w:r.w:t: Project Brief | Built by Anubhav | May 2026 | v1.0 Blueprint

SAGE is a standalone AI-powered security tool. It monitors codebases, fetches CVEs daily, statically analyzes vulnerable code patterns, generates patches, validates them, and raises GitHub PRs — without manual intervention. It is named after the Security Analysis & Graph Engine at its core. The internal Knowledge Graph module is codenamed Synapse.
Iron Man JARVIS holographic code view → Code Knowledge Graph

Anubhav has multiple personal tools and GitHub repos. CVEs arrive constantly. GitHub Dependabot notifies sometimes — but it doesn't fix, doesn't understand code context, and misses transitive dependencies. Manually tracking which repo uses which library at which version, then patching it, is tedious and unrealistic at scale.
One tool that silently watches all repos
When a CVE arrives, it figures out if your code is actually affected
If yes — it patches the code, validates the fix, and raises a PR
You only get involved when human judgment is genuinely needed
Simple problem. SAGE is the proper engineering answer to it.

SAGE is built in modules. Each module is independent and swappable. The core loop: CVE Fetch → Stack Filter → Version Check → Knowledge Graph Query → Static Analysis → LLM Analysis → Patch Generate → Test Validate → Final Security Check → GitHub PR.
Map codebase — functions, deps, call chains
Detect vulnerable code patterns without payloads
Confirm vulnerability, reason about code context
Generate secure rewrite of vulnerable function
Final pass — ensure patch didn't introduce new issues
Raise PR with CVE ref, diff, explanation

Synapse is the brain of SAGE. Inspired by the Iron Man JARVIS holographic code view — where only the relevant system fires when queried, not the entire suit. The same principle applies here: build the graph once, query only what's relevant per CVE.
Only relevant functions fetched — not full codebase
Codebase doesn't re-scan — graph is pre-built
Day 1 only: Scan entire codebase → build Knowledge Graph → store in NetworkX/Neo4j
On CVE arrival: Query graph for relevant nodes — no re-scan
Only affected functions sent to LLM — fast, cheap, accurate
Graph updates only when new code is pushed — not on every CVE
This is the most critical missing piece in naive CVE tools. Real vulnerabilities (Log4Shell being the canonical example) are almost never in direct dependencies — they live in transitive chains.

SAGE maps the full chain. Tools like pip-audit or cyclonedx-python extract the complete dependency tree — not just top-level requirements.txt. Without this, SAGE would miss the majority of real-world vulnerabilities.
Source: NVD API (free, official). Fetch daily by published date.
Stack filter: Only process CVEs relevant to Python, Node, React, etc.
Version pinning: Check requirements.txt / package.json. CVE affects 2.28.0? You have 2.31.0? Skip. Saves ~60-70% of unnecessary LLM calls.
Use packaging library (Python) for PEP 440 compliant version range matching. Never manual string comparison — '2.9.0' > '2.10.0' is wrong as a string.
SQLite: Track processed CVEs. Never process the same CVE twice.
CVE arrives → query Knowledge Graph for relevant nodes.
Returns only the functions and modules that use the affected library.
Full transitive chain included — not just direct callers.
This is where SAGE's approach differs from naive tools. Instead of running payloads against code, SAGE checks if the code is structurally vulnerable — independent of any payload.
# Vulnerable — string concatenation with user input
query = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ' + user_input

Semgrep has ready-made rules for OWASP Top 10, SQL injection, XSS, command injection, path traversal and more. SAGE maps CVE → CWE → Semgrep rule set, then runs the scan. Payload databases (SecLists, PayloadsAllTheThings) are used only for confirmation — not primary detection.
Send structured CVE data (not free text) + code chunk to Claude Sonnet.
Structured input includes: CVE ID, affected versions array, fixed version, vulnerability type, attack vector. This eliminates hallucination from free-text descriptions.
LLM confirms vulnerability, explains reasoning, and generates a secure rewrite.
Confidence score returned — low confidence routes to human review, not auto-apply.
Two-layer validation before any patch is applied:
Existing tests: Run the repo's existing pytest / jest suite against patched code.

CVE-specific tests: LLM generates attack-specific test cases for the vulnerability type. Existing tests often don't cover the specific attack vector — a SQL injection fix needs to be tested with actual injection payloads, not just 'login works'.
For well-known CWE types (CWE-89, CWE-79, etc.): Use payload databases (SecLists, PayloadsAllTheThings) instead of LLM-generated payloads — battle-tested, no hallucination.
Novel CWEs: Fall back to LLM-generated test cases.
This is the most important step. A security tool that introduces new vulnerabilities while fixing old ones is worse than no tool at all.
Semgrep re-scans the patched code — did the patch introduce a new pattern?
LLM reviews the patch: 'Did fixing this break anything else? Any new attack surface?'
Both pass → raise GitHub PR automatically.
Either fails → hard stop. Flag for human review. No auto-apply.
Daily CVE feed with structured metadata
Daily cron trigger, on-push graph update

Medical ethics applied to security tooling. A patch that introduces a new vulnerability is worse than no patch. This is why the final security check exists and why human-in-the-loop is mandatory for critical changes.

Check if the code structure is vulnerable before running any payloads. Structural analysis is payload-independent — new attack variants don't require new payload lists. Semgrep catches patterns, not just known exploits.

A security tool that is itself insecure is worse than no tool. SAGE handles sensitive data — GitHub tokens, Claude API keys, CVE data, code patches. Every attack surface must be accounted for from day one.
API keys stored in .env file — never hardcoded, never committed.
.env in .gitignore — mandatory, enforced before first commit.
python-dotenv for loading — no os.environ direct writes in code.
Pickle rejected — uses __reduce__ internally, arbitrary code execution possible if file is tampered.
Joblib rejected — internally uses pickle, same vulnerability. Performance benefit only, not a security improvement.
JSON only for graph storage — no code execution possible. Worst case: malformed data, not RCE.
JSON schema validation mandatory on every load — reject malformed input before processing.
CVE ID with SQL payload injected as string value
Schema validation — strict regex on CVE ID field
10MB strings or 10M item arrays in response
maxLength and maxItems constraints in schema
10000 levels deep — stack overflow on parse
version field is null instead of string array
Strict type checking in schema — reject unexpected types
CVE data from NVD API — treated as untrusted. Schema validated before any processing.
Repo paths — validated against path traversal (../../etc/passwd style attacks).
GitHub API responses — sanitized before use. Never passed directly to shell commands.
LLM output — treated as untrusted code. Never auto-applied without test gate.
Secrets never logged — API keys, tokens, passwords stripped before any log write.
CVE data logged — full audit trail of what was checked.
Patch diffs logged — every change tracked with timestamp.
LLM prompts/responses logged — for debugging and audit.

The goal is zero interruptions for things SAGE can confidently handle, and one clean morning digest for things that genuinely need human judgment. Asking permission for every action defeats the purpose of the tool.
Core Rule — Tests Decide, Not Version Numbers
Earlier thinking: auto-apply minor version updates, human review major updates. This is wrong. Minor version updates can have breaking changes too. Version number is not a reliable safety signal.
SAGE runs test suite against updated code
Tests pass? → Auto apply. No interruption.
Tests fail? → Hold. Add to morning digest.
SAGE runs silently overnight. One summary in the morning — not 20 permission requests at 2am.
No test suite = no auto-apply. This is a hard rule. But SAGE does not expect Anubhav to write all tests from scratch.
Business logic — does the app work correctly?
Attack vectors — is the specific vulnerability actually fixed?
Most of Anubhav's repos currently have no test suite. SAGE's approach:
SAGE generates a test template for each function — Anubhav fills in expected values only.
Security tests (attack-specific) — SAGE generates fully, no input needed from Anubhav.
For known CWE types (SQL injection, XSS, etc.) — payload databases used, not LLM guesses.
For novel CWEs — LLM generates test cases as fallback.
Without functional tests → patch still generated, but flagged for mandatory manual review. No auto-apply.
SAGE eats its own dog food. Every security check SAGE runs on other codebases, it runs on itself.
After every module is built — Semgrep runs on that module's code before moving to next phase.
SAGE monitors its own requirements.txt for CVEs — it will patch itself.
SAGE uses latest library versions — verified on PyPI at time of writing each module.
Library versions pinned in requirements.txt — never floating (requests>=2.0 is banned, requests==2.32.3 only).

langchain ← banned, no version = whatever pip feels like
